question: How Do I Fix a Broken or Missing .htaccess File?
metaDescription: WordPress regenerates the standard rewrite rules automatically on a Permalinks settings save — this alone fixes most missing .htaccess problems.
shortAnswer: On Apache hosting, WordPress's standard rewrite rules live in the site's .htaccess file, and a missing or corrupted file typically breaks clean URLs sitewide, including WooCommerce pages, producing widespread 404 errors. Simply visiting Settings → Permalinks and clicking Save regenerates the standard WordPress rewrite block automatically, which resolves the majority of cases without needing to manually recreate the file.

bodyHtml:
Why This Happens

The .htaccess file, on Apache-based hosting, contains the rewrite rules that translate clean, readable URLs into the actual WordPress page requests behind them. This file can go missing or become corrupted from a server migration, a hosting-side reset, a security plugin's own rewrite rules conflicting with WordPress's, or simply a manual editing mistake — and when it's broken, nearly every non-homepage URL on the site can start returning a 404, WooCommerce pages included.

Common Causes

  • A server migration or restore that didn't correctly transfer the existing .htaccess file, or reset it to a generic default.
  • A security plugin or CDN writing its own rules into .htaccess in a way that conflicts with or overwrites WordPress's expected block.
  • Manual editing (adding a custom rule, a redirect) that introduced a syntax error, breaking the whole file's processing.
  • File permission issues preventing WordPress from writing to the file when it needs to regenerate rules automatically.

How to Fix It

  1. Go to Settings → Permalinks and click Save without changing anything — this forces WordPress to regenerate its standard rewrite block, resolving most cases.
  2. If that doesn't work, check file permissions on .htaccess and its containing directory, ensuring WordPress can actually write to it.
  3. If a plugin's own rules are suspected of conflicting, temporarily deactivate it and regenerate permalinks again to test.
  4. As a last resort, manually recreate the file with WordPress's standard rewrite block, available in the WordPress documentation, then re-add any legitimate custom rules afterward.
